nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Matter is particulate
nodes.outcome: State that all matter is made up of tiny particles

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Matter has mass and volume
nodes.outcome: Identify that anything occupying space and having mass is matter

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Space between particles
nodes.outcome: Conclude from dissolving salt in water without a level change that particles have space between them

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Everyday mixing examples
nodes.outcome: Give everyday examples like tea, coffee or lemonade showing space between particles of different substances

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Serial dilution observation
nodes.outcome: Describe how repeated serial dilution still shows colour, indicating particles are extremely small

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Dilution factor calculation
nodes.outcome: Calculate the dilution factor after successive dilutions of a coloured solution

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Estimate particle size limit
nodes.outcome: Estimate an upper limit for the size of particles from dilution observations (about 10^-9 m)

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Three characteristics of particles
nodes.outcome: List the three main characteristics: particles have space between them, move continuously and attract each other

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Particles keep moving
nodes.outcome: State that particles of matter are continuously moving because they possess kinetic energy

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define diffusion
nodes.outcome: Define diffusion as intermixing of particles due to their continuous motion

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Temperature affects diffusion
nodes.outcome: Explain that diffusion becomes faster at higher temperature due to increased kinetic energy

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Smell travels by diffusion
nodes.outcome: Relate everyday observations like smelling hot food across a room to diffusion of gaseous particles

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Gases diffuse into liquids
nodes.outcome: Explain how gases like oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse into water and support aquatic life

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Interparticle attraction
nodes.outcome: State that particles of matter attract each other with a force that keeps them together

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Compare cohesive forces
nodes.outcome: Compare the force of attraction between particles in iron, chalk and a rubber band and order them by strength

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Why water stream resists cutting
nodes.outcome: Explain why a stream of water cannot be easily cut with fingers using interparticle attraction

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Name three states
nodes.outcome: Name the three physical states of matter: solid, liquid and gas

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Same substance, states differ
nodes.outcome: Explain that ice, water and steam are the same substance in different states differing only in particle arrangement

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Properties of solids
nodes.outcome: List properties of solids: definite shape, distinct boundaries, fixed volume and negligible compressibility

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Why solids are rigid
nodes.outcome: Explain rigidity of solids by tightly packed particles held by strong forces of attraction

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Solids resist shape change
nodes.outcome: Predict what happens when force is applied to a solid and justify why it breaks rather than flows

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Properties of liquids
nodes.outcome: Describe properties of liquids: fixed volume, no fixed shape, fluidity and taking the shape of the container

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Liquid particle arrangement
nodes.outcome: Compare the spacing and attraction of liquid particles with those in solids to explain flow

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Density of states
nodes.outcome: Order solids, liquids and gases by density and explain using particle packing

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Gases are highly compressible
nodes.outcome: Explain the high compressibility of gases compared to solids and liquids using large interparticle spaces

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Compressed gas applications
nodes.outcome: Identify everyday applications of compressed gases such as LPG cylinders and CNG vehicles

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Gases fill container
nodes.outcome: Explain why gases expand to fill their container completely and exert pressure on its walls

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Kinetic energy rises with temperature
nodes.outcome: State that kinetic energy of particles increases with temperature for all states of matter

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Interconversion diagram
nodes.outcome: Sketch and label a diagram showing melting, boiling/fusion, condensation, solidification and sublimation between the three states

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Ice to steam trace
nodes.outcome: Trace the transformation ice -> water -> steam naming each change of state along the temperature path

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define melting point
nodes.outcome: Define melting point as the temperature at which a solid melts to become a liquid at atmospheric pressure

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define boiling point
nodes.outcome: Define boiling point as the temperature at which a liquid boils throughout its bulk at atmospheric pressure

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Latent heat of fusion
nodes.outcome: Define latent heat of fusion and state its SI unit, giving the value for ice

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Latent heat of vaporization
nodes.outcome: Define latent heat of vaporization and give the value for water

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Temperature constant while changing state
nodes.outcome: Explain why thermometer reading stays constant during melting or boiling even though heat is supplied

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Sublimation examples
nodes.outcome: Name substances like camphor and naphthalene that undergo sublimation and describe the experiment showing it

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Pressure liquefies gases
nodes.outcome: Explain how applying pressure and lowering temperature can liquefy a gas

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Dry ice
nodes.outcome: Describe why solid carbon dioxide is called dry ice and how it converts directly to gas

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define evaporation
nodes.outcome: Define evaporation as conversion of a liquid into vapour below its boiling point

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Evaporation is surface phenomenon
nodes.outcome: Explain evaporation as a surface phenomenon where only surface particles escape

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Boiling vs evaporation
nodes.outcome: Distinguish boiling from evaporation on the basis of temperature, location (bulk vs surface) and speed

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Four factors of evaporation
nodes.outcome: List the four factors affecting rate of evaporation: surface area, temperature, humidity and wind speed

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Predict evaporation changes
nodes.outcome: Predict whether wet clothes dry faster or slower when humidity, wind, temperature or spread-out area changes

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Evaporation causes cooling
nodes.outcome: Explain cooling during evaporation using energy absorbed from surroundings by escaping particles

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Earthen pot cooling
nodes.outcome: Explain why water remains cool in an earthen pot (matka) using evaporation through pores

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Acetone cools palm
nodes.outcome: Explain the cooling sensation when acetone or perfume evaporates from skin

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Cotton clothes in summer
nodes.outcome: Apply evaporation cooling to explain why cotton clothes are preferred in summer

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define mixture
nodes.outcome: Define a mixture as a physical combination of two or more substances that are not chemically combined.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Distinguish pure vs mixture
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between pure substances (e.g., water, sugar) and mixtures (e.g., salt water, air) by stating that pure substances have fixed composition and properties, while mixtures have variable composition.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Examples of mixtures
nodes.outcome: Give examples of mixtures from daily life, such as air, milk, and soil.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Mixture variable composition
nodes.outcome: Explain that the composition of a mixture is not fixed and can vary.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Classify mixtures
nodes.outcome: Classify a given mixture as homogeneous (uniform composition throughout) or heterogeneous (non-uniform composition).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Prepare salt solution
nodes.outcome: Describe the preparation of a salt solution by dissolving salt in water, noting that the salt particles are not visible and the mixture is uniform.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Prepare sand and water
nodes.outcome: Describe the preparation of a sand-and-water mixture, noting that sand particles are visible and settle over time.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Examples of mixture types
nodes.outcome: Give examples of homogeneous mixtures (e.g., salt water, sugar solution) and heterogeneous mixtures (e.g., oil and water, sand and water).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define solute, solvent, solution
nodes.outcome: Define solute (the substance that dissolves), solvent (the substance that dissolves the solute), and solution (the homogeneous mixture of solute and solvent).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify solute and solvent
nodes.outcome: Identify the solute and solvent in a given solution (e.g., in salt water, salt is solute, water is solvent).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Properties of solutions
nodes.outcome: List the key properties of solutions: particle size < 1 nm, stable, do not scatter light, cannot be separated by filtration.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Water as universal solvent
nodes.outcome: Describe water as a universal solvent because it dissolves many substances.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Factors affecting solubility
nodes.outcome: List factors that affect solubility: temperature, pressure, and nature of solute and solvent.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Temperature effect on solubility
nodes.outcome: Explain that solubility of solids generally increases with temperature, while solubility of gases decreases with temperature.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate mass percentage
nodes.outcome: Calculate the mass-by-mass percentage of a solution using the formula: (mass of solute / mass of solution) × 100.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate mass of solute
nodes.outcome: Calculate the mass of solute in a solution given its mass-by-mass percentage and the total mass of the solution.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define saturated and unsaturated
nodes.outcome: Define a saturated solution as a solution that cannot dissolve any more solute at a given temperature, and an unsaturated solution as one that can still dissolve more solute.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Heating saturated solution
nodes.outcome: Describe that heating a saturated solution can allow it to dissolve more solute, making it unsaturated.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define supersaturated solution
nodes.outcome: Define a supersaturated solution as a solution that contains more dissolved solute than a saturated solution at the same temperature, and is unstable.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define suspension
nodes.outcome: Define a suspension as a heterogeneous mixture in which solute particles are visible and do not dissolve.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Properties of suspensions
nodes.outcome: Describe the properties of suspensions: particle size > 100 nm, visible to naked eye, scatter light, settle on standing, can be separated by filtration.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Examples of suspensions
nodes.outcome: Give examples of suspensions such as muddy water, chalk powder in water, and paint.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Suspension instability
nodes.outcome: Explain that suspensions are unstable and the particles settle over time due to gravity.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define colloid
nodes.outcome: Define a colloid as a heterogeneous mixture with particle size between 1-100 nm, and identify the dispersed phase (the substance present in smaller amount) and dispersion medium (the substance in larger amount).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Types of colloids
nodes.outcome: Give examples of different types of colloids: sol (ink), gel (jelly), emulsion (milk), foam (whipped cream).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify dispersed phase and medium
nodes.outcome: Identify the dispersed phase and dispersion medium in a given colloid (e.g., in milk, fat droplets dispersed in water).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Colloid stability
nodes.outcome: Explain that colloidal particles do not settle due to Brownian motion and are stable.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Tyndall effect
nodes.outcome: Explain the Tyndall effect as the scattering of light by colloidal particles, and give an example such as a beam of light passing through a milk solution.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Separation of colloids
nodes.outcome: Describe that colloids can be separated by centrifugation, not by filtration.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define physical change
nodes.outcome: Define a physical change as a change that does not produce a new substance and is usually reversible.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define chemical change
nodes.outcome: Define a chemical change as a change that produces one or more new substances and is usually irreversible.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Classify physical vs chemical
nodes.outcome: Classify a given change (e.g., melting, rusting, burning) as physical or chemical based on criteria of new substance formation and reversibility.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Indicators of chemical change
nodes.outcome: List indicators of a chemical change: change in color, evolution of gas, change in temperature, formation of a precipitate.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Distinguish changes with examples
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between physical and chemical changes using examples like boiling water (physical) and electrolysis of water (chemical).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Classify pure substances
nodes.outcome: Classify pure substances into elements (cannot be broken down into simpler substances) and compounds (can be broken down into elements by chemical means).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define element
nodes.outcome: Define an element as a pure substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical means.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define compound
nodes.outcome: Define a compound as a pure substance composed of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Examples of elements and compounds
nodes.outcome: Give examples of elements (e.g., hydrogen, oxygen, iron) and compounds (e.g., water, carbon dioxide).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Classify elements into metals/nonmetals
nodes.outcome: Describe the classification of elements into metals, non-metals, and metalloids based on their properties.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Boyle and Lavoisier on elements
nodes.outcome: State that Robert Boyle defined an element as a substance that cannot be broken down into simpler substances, and Lavoisier defined it as a substance that cannot be decomposed by chemical means.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Properties of metals
nodes.outcome: List typical physical properties of metals: lustre, ductility, malleability, conductivity, sonority.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Properties of nonmetals
nodes.outcome: List typical physical properties of non-metals: non-lustrous, brittle, poor conductors of heat and electricity.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Characteristics of metalloids
nodes.outcome: State that metalloids have properties intermediate between metals and non-metals, e.g., silicon is a semiconductor.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Compound properties differ
nodes.outcome: Explain that the properties of a compound (e.g., iron sulfide) are different from the properties of its constituent elements (iron and sulfur).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Mixture vs compound: iron and sulfur
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between a mixture of iron and sulfur (which can be separated by physical means, retains properties of iron and sulfur) and the compound iron sulfide (which has different properties and cannot be separated by physical means).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Lavoisier and conservation of mass
nodes.outcome: State the Law of Conservation of Mass and identify Antoine Lavoisier as the scientist who established it.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Proust and constant proportions
nodes.outcome: State the Law of Constant Proportions and identify Joseph Proust as the scientist who proposed it.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Verify conservation of mass
nodes.outcome: Verify the Law of Conservation of Mass by calculating the total mass of reactants and products from given chemical reaction data.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Sealed flask experiment
nodes.outcome: Describe the experiment demonstrating the Law of Conservation of Mass using the reaction of barium chloride and sodium sulfate in a sealed flask.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Constant proportions in water
nodes.outcome: Explain the Law of Constant Proportions using the example of water, stating the 1:8 mass ratio of hydrogen to oxygen.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate mass from ratio
nodes.outcome: Calculate the mass of one element in a compound given the mass of the other element and their fixed combining ratio.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define atom
nodes.outcome: Define an atom as the building block of all matter.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Dalton’s postulate: matter made of atoms
nodes.outcome: State that according to Dalton, all matter is made up of tiny indivisible particles called atoms.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Dalton’s postulate: identical atoms of same element
nodes.outcome: State the Dalton postulate that atoms of a given element are identical in mass and chemical properties.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Dalton’s postulate: atoms combine in simple ratios
nodes.outcome: State the Dalton postulate that atoms of different elements combine in simple whole-number ratios to form compounds.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Dalton’s postulate: atoms rearranged in reactions
nodes.outcome: State the Dalton postulate that in a chemical reaction, atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Recall IUPAC symbols
nodes.outcome: Recall the modern symbols of common elements (H, He, C, N, O, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, K, Ca, Fe, Cu, Zn, Ag, I, Pb, Au, Hg) as approved by IUPAC.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Symbol origin from Latin names
nodes.outcome: Explain that some element symbols are derived from their Latin names (e.g., Fe from Ferrum, Na from Natrium, K from Kalium, Cu from Cuprum, Ag from Argentum, Au from Aurum, Hg from Hydrargyrum).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define atomic mass unit
nodes.outcome: Define atomic mass unit (u) as 1/12th the mass of a carbon-12 atom.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Carbon-12 standard for atomic mass
nodes.outcome: Explain why carbon-12 is used as the standard reference for atomic mass, citing its stability and convenient mass.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Monoatomic vs. molecules/ions
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between elements that exist as monoatomic (e.g., noble gases) and those that exist as molecules or ions (e.g., H2, O2, Na+, Cl-).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Why atoms cannot exist independently
nodes.outcome: State that most atoms cannot exist independently under normal conditions because they are reactive and combine with other atoms to achieve stability.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define molecule
nodes.outcome: Define a molecule as a group of two or more atoms chemically bonded together.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Atomicity with examples
nodes.outcome: Explain atomicity and give examples of monoatomic (He), diatomic (O2), triatomic (O3), and polyatomic (P4) molecules.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Molecules of elements defined
nodes.outcome: Define molecules of elements as containing atoms of only one element.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Classify molecular elements by atomicity
nodes.outcome: Classify molecules of elements as monoatomic, diatomic, triatomic, or polyatomic based on the number of atoms present.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Molecules of compounds defined
nodes.outcome: Define molecules of compounds as containing atoms of two or more different elements.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Atom ratio in water and ammonia
nodes.outcome: State the ratio by number of atoms in a water (H2O) molecule as 2:1 (H:O) and in an ammonia (NH3) molecule as 1:3 (N:H).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define ions, cations, anions
nodes.outcome: Define ions as charged particles, cations as positively charged ions, and anions as negatively charged ions.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Common polyatomic ions
nodes.outcome: List the constituent elements and charges of common polyatomic ions: ammonium (NH4+), carbonate (CO3^2-), sulphate (SO4^2-), nitrate (NO3-), hydroxide (OH-), and phosphate (PO4^3-).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define valency
nodes.outcome: Define valency as the combining capacity of an element, measured by the number of hydrogen atoms it can combine with or displace.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Balance charges using valency
nodes.outcome: Apply the rule of writing chemical formulae by crossing over valencies to balance the total positive and negative charges when combining ions.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Write formulas of binary compounds
nodes.outcome: Write the chemical formula of binary compounds (e.g., NaCl, MgO, H2O, CO2) using the valencies of the constituent elements.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Translate compound names to formulas
nodes.outcome: Translate common compound names (e.g., sodium oxide, calcium chloride, aluminium oxide) into their correct molecular formulas.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define molecular mass
nodes.outcome: Define molecular mass as the sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in a molecule.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate molecular mass
nodes.outcome: Calculate the molecular mass of chemical compounds from given atomic masses (e.g., H2O, CO2, CH4, C2H5OH).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Compare molecular masses of H2O and CO2
nodes.outcome: Compare the molecular masses of water (H2O) and carbon dioxide (CO2) and state which is heavier.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define formula unit mass
nodes.outcome: Define formula unit mass as the sum of atomic masses of all atoms in a formula unit of an ionic compound, and state that it is used for compounds that do not exist as discrete molecules.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate formula unit mass
nodes.outcome: Calculate the formula unit mass of sodium chloride (NaCl) and calcium chloride (CaCl2) from given atomic masses.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Formula unit mass calculation is same
nodes.outcome: Explain that the formula unit mass is calculated in the same manner as molecular mass, by summing atomic masses of all atoms in the formula unit.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define mole
nodes.outcome: Define a mole as the amount of substance that contains 6.022 × 10^23 entities (atoms, molecules, ions, or particles).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Avogadro number
nodes.outcome: State Avogadro number as 6.022 × 10^23 and identify it as the number of particles in one mole of any substance.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate number of particles
nodes.outcome: Calculate the number of particles (atoms, molecules, or ions) given the number of moles or mass of a substance using Avogadro number.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate mass from moles
nodes.outcome: Calculate the mass of a substance given the number of moles and its molar mass.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate moles from mass
nodes.outcome: Calculate the number of moles of a substance given its mass and molar mass.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define molar mass
nodes.outcome: Define molar mass as the mass of one mole of a substance, numerically equal to the molecular or formula mass in grams.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Relate mass, moles, and particles
nodes.outcome: Relate the mass, number of moles, and number of particles of a substance using the formulas: mass = moles × molar mass; number of particles = moles × Avogadro number.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Valency of common elements
nodes.outcome: Recall the valencies of common elements: H(1), O(2), Na(1), Mg(2), Al(3), C(4), N(3), Cl(1), Ca(2), Fe(2,3), etc.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Write formulas with polyatomic ions
nodes.outcome: Write the chemical formula of compounds containing polyatomic ions (e.g., NaOH, CaCO3, NH4Cl, Al2(SO4)3) by balancing charges.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Dalton: atoms of different elements differ
nodes.outcome: State the Dalton postulate that atoms of different elements have different masses and chemical properties.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Dalton: atoms are indivisible
nodes.outcome: State the Dalton postulate that atoms are indivisible and cannot be created or destroyed.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate molar mass
nodes.outcome: Calculate the molar mass of a compound by summing the atomic masses of all atoms in its formula and expressing the result in g/mol.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Static electricity and atoms
nodes.outcome: Explain that static electricity experiments (like rubbing a comb on dry hair) indicate that atoms contain charged particles.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Electron discovery
nodes.outcome: Identify that the electron was the first subatomic particle discovered by J.J. Thomson.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Atom neutrality
nodes.outcome: Explain that an atom is electrically neutral because the number of protons equals the number of electrons.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Three subatomic particles
nodes.outcome: List the three major subatomic particles: protons, neutrons, and electrons.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Proton properties
nodes.outcome: State the charge and approximate mass of a proton (1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, 1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Electron properties
nodes.outcome: State the charge and approximate mass of an electron (-1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C, 9.1×10⁻³¹ kg).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Compare proton and electron
nodes.outcome: Compare the charge and mass of a proton with those of an electron (opposite charge, mass ~1840 times greater for proton).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Plum pudding model
nodes.outcome: Describe Thomson's 'plum pudding' (or watermelon) model of the atom, including a sphere of positive charge with embedded electrons.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Thomson's postulates
nodes.outcome: State the two major postulates of Thomson's model: (i) atom is a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded, (ii) atom is electrically neutral.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Alternate names for Thomson model
nodes.outcome: State that Thomson's model is also known as the plum pudding or watermelon model.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Alpha particle definition
nodes.outcome: Define an alpha particle as a positively charged helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons, +2 charge).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Rutherford experiment setup
nodes.outcome: Describe the setup of Rutherford's alpha-particle scattering experiment, including the gold foil, alpha source, and detector.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Rutherford's observations
nodes.outcome: State the three observations of Rutherford's experiment: most alpha particles pass through, some are deflected, very few bounce back.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Conclusion about nucleus
nodes.outcome: Conclude from Rutherford's observations that the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Conclusion about empty space
nodes.outcome: Conclude from Rutherford's observations that most of the atom is empty space.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Rutherford model instability
nodes.outcome: Explain why Rutherford's model predicted unstable electron orbits: an electron in circular orbit would continuously radiate energy and spiral into the nucleus.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Bohr's solution to instability
nodes.outcome: Describe how Bohr's model overcomes the instability of Rutherford's model by introducing quantized energy levels (electrons can only occupy specific orbits without radiating energy).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Discrete orbits in Bohr model
nodes.outcome: State that electrons can only occupy discrete orbits (shells) with fixed energy in Bohr's model.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Sketch Bohr's energy levels
nodes.outcome: Sketch the first four energy shells (K, L, M, N) corresponding to principal quantum numbers n=1, 2, 3, 4.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Neutron discovery
nodes.outcome: Identify the neutron as a neutral subatomic particle discovered by James Chadwick.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Mass concentration in nucleus
nodes.outcome: State that the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus, which contains protons and neutrons.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Bohr-Bury 2n² rule
nodes.outcome: State the Bohr-Bury rule for maximum number of electrons in a shell: 2n².

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate shell capacity
nodes.outcome: Calculate the maximum number of electrons for the first three shells (n=1,2,3) using 2n².

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Shell filling order
nodes.outcome: State that electrons fill shells in order of increasing energy (K, L, M, ...) and that the outermost shell can hold at most 8 electrons.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Apply 2n² to first 18 elements
nodes.outcome: Apply the Bohr-Bury rules to determine the electron configuration of any element with atomic number up to 18.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Draw atomic structure: H
nodes.outcome: Draw the schematic atomic structure of hydrogen (nucleus with 1 proton, 1 electron in K shell).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Draw atomic structure: He
nodes.outcome: Draw the schematic atomic structure of helium (nucleus with 2 protons, 2 neutrons, 2 electrons in K shell).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Draw atomic structure: Na
nodes.outcome: Draw the schematic atomic structure of sodium (nucleus with 11 protons, 12 neutrons; electrons: 2 in K, 8 in L, 1 in M).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define valence electrons
nodes.outcome: Define valence electrons as the electrons in the outermost shell of an atom.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Determine valence electrons
nodes.outcome: Determine the number of valence electrons from the electron configuration of an element.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Octet rule
nodes.outcome: State the octet rule: atoms tend to achieve a full outermost shell of eight electrons (or two for H, He) for stability.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define valency
nodes.outcome: Define valency as the combining capacity of an element, determined by the number of electrons it can gain, lose, or share to achieve a full outer shell.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Valency of noble gases
nodes.outcome: State that noble gases have zero valency because their outermost shell is full (except He with 2).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate valency for first 18 elements
nodes.outcome: Calculate the valency of elements from the first 18 elements based on their electron configurations (e.g., Na=1, Cl=1, O=2, etc.).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Valency vs valence electrons
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between valency and the number of valence electrons for an element (e.g., Na has 1 valence electron and valency 1, O has 6 valence electrons and valency 2).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define atomic number
nodes.outcome: Define atomic number (Z) as the number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify element from atomic number
nodes.outcome: Identify an element given its atomic number using the periodic table.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define mass number
nodes.outcome: Define mass number (A) as the total number of protons and neutrons in the nucleus.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define nucleons
nodes.outcome: State that protons and neutrons are collectively called nucleons.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate mass number
nodes.outcome: Calculate the mass number of an atom given the numbers of protons and neutrons.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Standard notation for element
nodes.outcome: Use standard notation to represent an element, e.g., ^A_Z X.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define isotopes
nodes.outcome: Define isotopes as atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different mass numbers.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Examples of isotopes
nodes.outcome: Give examples of isotopes: hydrogen-1, hydrogen-2, hydrogen-3; carbon-12, carbon-14.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate neutrons in isotope
nodes.outcome: Calculate the number of neutrons in an isotope given its atomic number and mass number.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Applications of isotopes
nodes.outcome: List applications of isotopes: uranium-235 in nuclear reactors, cobalt-60 in cancer treatment, iodine-131 in thyroid diagnostics.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define isobars
nodes.outcome: Define isobars as atoms of different elements with the same mass number but different atomic numbers.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify isobars
nodes.outcome: Identify isobars from a list of atomic numbers and mass numbers (e.g., Ar-40, K-40, Ca-40).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Compare isotopes and isobars
nodes.outcome: Compare isotopes and isobars in terms of atomic number, mass number, and chemical properties (isotopes have same chemical properties, isobars different).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Cells as basic unit of life
nodes.outcome: State that cells are the basic structural and functional units of all living organisms.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Hooke's discovery of cells
nodes.outcome: Describe how Robert Hooke observed cells in a thin slice of cork using a primitive microscope and named them 'cells'.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Three main regions of a cell
nodes.outcome: Identify the plasma membrane, nucleus, and cytoplasm as the three main functional regions of a cell.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Roles of the three cell regions
nodes.outcome: State that the plasma membrane encloses the cell, the nucleus controls cellular activities, and the cytoplasm is the site of many metabolic reactions.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Selective permeability of plasma membrane
nodes.outcome: Define selective permeability as the property of the plasma membrane that allows some substances to pass through while preventing others.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Composition of plasma membrane
nodes.outcome: State that the plasma membrane is composed of a bilayer of lipids with embedded proteins.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Diffusion across cell membrane
nodes.outcome: Define diffusion as the movement of molecules from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration across a cell membrane.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Definition of osmosis
nodes.outcome: Define osmosis as the movement of water molecules through a selectively permeable membrane from a region of high water concentration to a region of low water concentration.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Movement across plasma membrane
nodes.outcome: Explain that substances like gases and water move across the plasma membrane by diffusion and osmosis, respectively.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Location of cell wall
nodes.outcome: Locate the cell wall as the outermost layer of a plant cell, lying outside the plasma membrane.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Composition of cell wall
nodes.outcome: State that the plant cell wall is mainly composed of cellulose.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Function of cell wall
nodes.outcome: State that the cell wall provides structural support and protection to the plant cell.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Plasmolysis
nodes.outcome: Define plasmolysis as the shrinkage of the cytoplasm away from the cell wall due to water loss when a plant cell is placed in a hypertonic solution.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Animal cell in hypotonic solution
nodes.outcome: Predict that an animal cell placed in a hypotonic solution will swell and may burst due to water entering the cell.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Animal cell in isotonic solution
nodes.outcome: Predict that an animal cell placed in an isotonic solution will remain unchanged because equal water movement occurs.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Animal cell in hypertonic solution
nodes.outcome: Predict that an animal cell placed in a hypertonic solution will shrink due to water leaving the cell.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Plant cell in hypotonic solution
nodes.outcome: Predict that a plant cell placed in a hypotonic solution becomes turgid due to water entry but does not burst because of the cell wall.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Plant cell in isotonic solution
nodes.outcome: Predict that a plant cell placed in an isotonic solution remains flaccid because no net water movement.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Plant cell in hypertonic solution
nodes.outcome: Predict that a plant cell placed in a hypertonic solution undergoes plasmolysis due to water leaving the cell.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Structure of nucleus
nodes.outcome: Describe the nucleus as having a nuclear membrane with pores, nucleolus, and chromatin (thread-like material).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Function of nucleus
nodes.outcome: State that the nucleus controls all cellular activities and contains genetic material (DNA) in the form of chromatin.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Function of nucleolus
nodes.outcome: Explain that the nucleolus is a dense region within the nucleus that produces ribosomes.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Chromosomes contain DNA
nodes.outcome: State that chromatin condenses to form chromosomes which contain DNA and proteins.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Prokaryotic vs eukaryotic cells
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between prokaryotic cells (lacking a nucleus with nuclear membrane) and eukaryotic cells (having a true nucleus with nuclear membrane).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Examples of prokaryotes
nodes.outcome: Give examples of prokaryotes (e.g., bacteria) and eukaryotes (e.g., plants, animals, fungi).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Specific prokaryotes: bacteria and cyanobacteria
nodes.outcome: State that bacteria and blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) are examples of prokaryotes.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Definition of cytoplasm
nodes.outcome: Define cytoplasm as the jelly-like fluid substance inside the plasma membrane that contains organelles.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Importance of cytoplasmic organelles
nodes.outcome: Explain that cytoplasmic organelles perform specialized functions that maintain cell life.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Types of endoplasmic reticulum
nodes.outcome: Identify the endoplasmic reticulum as a network of membranes and distinguish between rough ER (with ribosomes) and smooth ER (without ribosomes).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Functions of rough and smooth ER
nodes.outcome: State that rough ER synthesizes proteins and smooth ER synthesizes lipids.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Function of ribosomes
nodes.outcome: Explain that ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis and can be attached to rough ER or free in cytoplasm.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Golgi apparatus
nodes.outcome: Identify the Golgi apparatus as stacks of membranes and state that it modifies, packages, and transports materials within the cell.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Lysosomes
nodes.outcome: Identify lysosomes as membrane-bound vesicles containing digestive enzymes and state that they break down waste and foreign substances.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Lysosomes as suicide bags
nodes.outcome: Explain that lysosomes can digest the cell itself by releasing enzymes when the cell is damaged, earning the nickname 'suicide bags'.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Mitochondria
nodes.outcome: Identify mitochondria as double-membrane organelles and state that they produce energy (ATP) through respiration.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Mitochondria as powerhouses
nodes.outcome: Explain that mitochondria are called the 'powerhouses of the cell' because they generate most of the cell's energy (ATP).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Types of plastids
nodes.outcome: Identify plastids as organelles in plant cells and distinguish three types: chloroplasts (green), chromoplasts (colored), and leucoplasts (colorless).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Functions of plastids
nodes.outcome: State that chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis, chromoplasts give color to flowers and fruits, and leucoplasts store starch, oils, and proteins.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Vacuoles
nodes.outcome: Identify vacuoles as fluid-filled sacs and state that they store substances and help in maintaining turgor pressure in plant cells.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Vacuole size comparison
nodes.outcome: Compare that plant cells usually have a large central vacuole, while animal cells have smaller vacuoles.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Comparison of animal and plant cells
nodes.outcome: Compare animal and plant cells by noting that plant cells have a cell wall, plastids, and a large central vacuole, while animal cells do not.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Cell size limited by surface area to volume ratio
nodes.outcome: State that cells are small because a larger surface area to volume ratio allows efficient diffusion of substances.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Endocytosis
nodes.outcome: Describe endocytosis as the process by which the plasma membrane engulfs external material to form a vesicle inside the cell.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Exocytosis
nodes.outcome: Describe exocytosis as the process by which a vesicle fuses with the plasma membrane to release its contents outside the cell.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Active vs passive transport
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between passive transport (diffusion, osmosis) which requires no energy, and active transport which uses energy to move substances against concentration gradient.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Fluid mosaic model
nodes.outcome: State that the plasma membrane is described by the fluid mosaic model, where lipids and proteins can move laterally.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Cell theory formulators
nodes.outcome: State that Schleiden and Schwann proposed the cell theory that all plants and animals are composed of cells.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Virchow's addition to cell theory
nodes.outcome: State that Rudolf Virchow modified the cell theory by stating that new cells arise from pre-existing cells (omnis cellula e cellula).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Contrast plant and animal tissues
nodes.outcome: Contrast plants and animals based on mobility, energy needs, and the resulting complexity of their tissues.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Localized vs uniform growth
nodes.outcome: Describe how plants have localized growth in specific regions (meristems) while animals have uniform growth throughout the body.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Classify plant tissues
nodes.outcome: Classify plant tissues into meristematic and permanent tissues.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Apical meristem location
nodes.outcome: Identify that apical meristem is located at the tips of roots and shoots.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Intercalary meristem location
nodes.outcome: Identify that intercalary meristem is located at the base of leaves and internodes in grasses.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Lateral meristem location
nodes.outcome: Identify that lateral meristem is located on the sides of the plant (cambium) and increases girth.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Meristematic cell characteristics
nodes.outcome: Describe the cellular characteristics of meristematic cells: thin cell walls, dense cytoplasm, large nuclei, and absence of vacuoles.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Role in length growth
nodes.outcome: Explain that apical and intercalary meristems are responsible for increase in length of the plant.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Role in girth growth
nodes.outcome: Explain that lateral meristem is responsible for increase in girth (width) of the plant.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define differentiation
nodes.outcome: Define differentiation as the process by which meristematic cells lose the ability to divide and become specialized permanent tissues.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Simple vs complex tissues
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between simple permanent tissues (made of one cell type) and complex permanent tissues (made of multiple cell types).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Parenchyma structure
nodes.outcome: Describe the structure of parenchyma cells: thin-walled, living, loosely packed with intercellular spaces.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Parenchyma function
nodes.outcome: Identify the functions of parenchyma: storage, photosynthesis (in chlorenchyma), and buoyancy (in aerenchyma).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Collenchyma structure
nodes.outcome: Describe the structure of collenchyma cells: living, elongated, with unevenly thickened cell walls, found under the epidermis.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Collenchyma function
nodes.outcome: State that collenchyma provides mechanical support and flexibility to plant parts.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Sclerenchyma structure
nodes.outcome: Describe the structure of sclerenchyma cells: dead cells with thick, lignified walls; narrow lumen; no intercellular spaces.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Sclerenchyma function
nodes.outcome: State that sclerenchyma provides strength and rigidity to plant organs and forms the protective covering of seeds and nuts.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Xylem structure
nodes.outcome: List the main cell types in xylem: tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, and xylem fibres.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Xylem function
nodes.outcome: Describe the primary function of xylem as conduction of water and minerals from roots to aerial parts.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Phloem structure
nodes.outcome: List the main cell types in phloem: sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma, and phloem fibres.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Phloem function
nodes.outcome: Describe the primary function of phloem as conduction of food (sugars) from leaves to other plant parts.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Name four animal tissue types
nodes.outcome: Name the four basic types of animal tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, and nervous.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Functions of animal tissues
nodes.outcome: State the primary function of each animal tissue: epithelium (covering/lining), connective (support/binding), muscle (contraction), and nervous (signal transmission).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: General epithelial tissue
nodes.outcome: Describe the general characteristics of epithelial tissue: tightly packed cells, little intercellular matrix, rests on a basement membrane, covers body surfaces and lines cavities.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Squamous epithelium identification
nodes.outcome: Identify squamous epithelium based on its flattened, scale-like cells.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Cuboidal epithelium identification
nodes.outcome: Identify cuboidal epithelium based on its cube-shaped cells.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Columnar epithelium identification
nodes.outcome: Identify columnar epithelium based on its tall, column-like cells.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Ciliated epithelium identification
nodes.outcome: Identify ciliated epithelium by the presence of hair-like cilia on the free surface.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Glandular epithelium identification
nodes.outcome: Identify glandular epithelium as specialized for secretion, often forming glands.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Epithelium shape-location correlation
nodes.outcome: Correlate epithelial shapes with typical locations: squamous (skin, alveoli), cuboidal (kidney tubules), columnar (intestine), ciliated (trachea), glandular (glands).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: General connective tissue
nodes.outcome: Describe the general characteristics of connective tissue: cells loosely arranged in an extracellular matrix, abundant matrix with fibers and ground substance.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Blood components and location
nodes.outcome: Describe the components (plasma, RBC, WBC, platelets) and locations (blood vessels, heart) of blood as a connective tissue.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Bone components and location
nodes.outcome: Describe the components (hard matrix of calcium phosphate, osteocytes) and locations (skeleton) of bone as a connective tissue.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Cartilage components and location
nodes.outcome: Describe the components (solid but flexible matrix, chondrocytes) and locations (nose, ear, joints) of cartilage as a connective tissue.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Areolar tissue components and location
nodes.outcome: Describe the components (fibroblasts, fibers, loose matrix) and locations (between skin and muscles, around organs) of areolar connective tissue.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Adipose tissue components and location
nodes.outcome: Describe the components (fat cells, little matrix) and locations (under skin, around kidneys) of adipose connective tissue.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Matrix determines properties
nodes.outcome: Explain that the physical properties of connective tissue (hardness, flexibility, fluidity) are determined by the nature of the extracellular matrix (solid, semi-solid, fluid).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Striated muscle characteristics
nodes.outcome: Describe striated (skeletal) muscle: long, cylindrical, multinucleated, unbranched, voluntary, with striations.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Unstriated muscle characteristics
nodes.outcome: Describe unstriated (smooth) muscle: spindle-shaped, uninucleated, no striations, involuntary.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Cardiac muscle characteristics
nodes.outcome: Describe cardiac muscle: striated, branched, uninucleated, with intercalated discs, involuntary, rhythmic contraction.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Compare muscle types
nodes.outcome: Compare striated, unstriated, and cardiac muscles in terms of structure, number of nuclei, presence of striations, branching, and type of control (voluntary/involuntary).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Neuron structure
nodes.outcome: Sketch and label a typical neuron showing cell body, dendrites, and axon.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Nerve impulse path
nodes.outcome: Trace the path of a nerve impulse: dendrites → cell body → axon → axon terminal → synapse → next neuron.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Nervous tissue function
nodes.outcome: State that nervous tissue is responsible for receiving stimuli and conducting nerve impulses for control and coordination.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Xylem cell types
nodes.outcome: List the four main cell types in xylem: tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres, and xylem parenchyma.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Phloem cell types
nodes.outcome: List the four main cell types in phloem: sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres, and phloem parenchyma.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Function of ciliated epithelium
nodes.outcome: Explain that ciliated epithelium in the respiratory tract moves mucus and trapped particles upward to be expelled.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Function of glandular epithelium
nodes.outcome: Explain that glandular epithelium secretes substances such as sweat, enzymes, or hormones.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define motion relative to reference
nodes.outcome: Define motion as a change in the position of an object with respect to a reference point.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify reference point
nodes.outcome: Identify the reference point or origin in a given description of motion.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Distinguish scalar and vector
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between scalar and vector quantities using distance (scalar) and displacement (vector) as examples.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define distance and displacement
nodes.outcome: Define distance as the total path length (scalar) and displacement as the change in position (vector) with direction.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate distance along straight line
nodes.outcome: Calculate the total distance traveled by an object moving along a straight line given its positions.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate displacement along straight line
nodes.outcome: Calculate the magnitude and direction of displacement for an object moving along a straight line from initial to final positions.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Example of zero displacement
nodes.outcome: Describe a situation where the displacement of an object is zero but the distance traveled is non-zero (e.g., returning to start point).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define uniform motion
nodes.outcome: Define uniform motion as motion where an object covers equal distances in equal intervals of time.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define non-uniform motion
nodes.outcome: Define non-uniform motion as motion where an object covers unequal distances in equal intervals of time.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Classify motion examples
nodes.outcome: Classify given examples of motion as uniform or non-uniform.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define speed and its SI unit
nodes.outcome: Define speed as distance traveled per unit time and state its SI unit as m/s.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate average speed
nodes.outcome: Calculate the average speed of an object given total distance and total time.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define velocity
nodes.outcome: Define velocity as displacement per unit time and write the formula v = s/t (with direction).

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Velocity change by speed or direction
nodes.outcome: Explain that velocity changes when either the speed or the direction of motion changes.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define acceleration and retardation
nodes.outcome: Define acceleration as the rate of change of velocity and classify positive acceleration as increase and negative (retardation) as decrease.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate average acceleration
nodes.outcome: Calculate average acceleration using the formula a = (v - u)/t.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Benefits of graphs in motion
nodes.outcome: List two benefits of using graphs to represent motion: visual comparison and easy calculation of speed/acceleration.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Plot distance-time graph
nodes.outcome: Plot a distance-time graph from given tabular data of time and distance.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate speed from distance-time slope
nodes.outcome: Calculate the speed of an object from the slope of a distance-time graph.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Plot velocity-time graph
nodes.outcome: Plot a velocity-time graph from given tabular data of velocity and time.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate distance from v-t area
nodes.outcome: Calculate the distance traveled by finding the area under a velocity-time graph.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Determine acceleration from v-t slope
nodes.outcome: Determine the acceleration from the slope of a velocity-time graph.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Interpret graph shape
nodes.outcome: Interpret the state of motion (rest, uniform, non-uniform) from the shape of a distance-time or velocity-time graph.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: State three equations of motion
nodes.outcome: State the three equations of motion for uniform acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + 0.5at^2, 2as = v^2 - u^2.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define variables in equations
nodes.outcome: Define each variable (u, v, a, t, s) in the three equations of motion.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Derive v = u + at
nodes.outcome: Derive the first equation of motion, v = u + at, from the slope of a velocity-time graph.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Solve v = u + at problems
nodes.outcome: Solve numerical problems using the first equation of motion, v = u + at.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Derive s = ut + 0.5at^2
nodes.outcome: Derive the second equation of motion, s = ut + 0.5at^2, using the area under a velocity-time graph.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate displacement from rest
nodes.outcome: Calculate the displacement of an object starting from rest under constant acceleration using the second equation of motion.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Derive 2as = v^2 - u^2
nodes.outcome: Derive the third equation of motion, 2as = v^2 - u^2, by calculating the area under a velocity-time graph.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Apply third equation to stopping distance
nodes.outcome: Apply the third equation of motion to determine the stopping distance when deceleration is known.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain circular motion acceleration
nodes.outcome: Explain that uniform circular motion is accelerated motion because the direction of velocity changes continuously.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate speed in uniform circular motion
nodes.outcome: Calculate the speed of an object in uniform circular motion using the formula v = 2πr/T.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define period in uniform circular motion
nodes.outcome: Define the time period T in uniform circular motion as the time taken to complete one revolution.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Distinguish speed and velocity
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between speed (scalar) and velocity (vector) in terms of magnitude and direction.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Choose appropriate equation
nodes.outcome: Choose the appropriate equation of motion (v=u+at, s=ut+0.5at^2, 2as=v^2-u^2) given the known and unknown variables in a problem.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify acceleration from v-t graph
nodes.outcome: Identify positive, negative, or zero acceleration from the slope of a velocity-time graph.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate average velocity
nodes.outcome: Calculate average velocity given total displacement and total time.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify uniform motion from table
nodes.outcome: Identify uniform motion from a table of distances at equal time intervals.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate displacement with multiple segments
nodes.outcome: Calculate the net displacement for an object moving along a straight line with multiple segments considering direction.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Convert units of speed
nodes.outcome: Convert speed from km/h to m/s and vice versa.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define instantaneous speed
nodes.outcome: Define instantaneous speed as the speed at a given instant.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Solve problems using second equation
nodes.outcome: Solve numerical problems using the second equation of motion, s = ut + 0.5at^2, for any given values.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Solve problems using third equation
nodes.outcome: Solve numerical problems using the third equation of motion, 2as = v^2 - u^2.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Assign sign to displacement
nodes.outcome: Assign a positive or negative sign to displacement based on the chosen direction along a straight line.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate distance with reversal
nodes.outcome: Calculate the total distance traveled when an object moves along a straight line and reverses direction.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Describe distance-time graph shapes
nodes.outcome: Describe the shape of a distance-time graph for an object at rest, in uniform motion, and in non-uniform motion.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Gravitational Force
nodes.outcome: State that gravitation is the universal attractive force acting between any two objects with mass in the universe

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Centripetal Force
nodes.outcome: Define centripetal force as the center-seeking force that keeps an object moving in a circular path

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Moon's Motion Around Earth
nodes.outcome: Explain that Earth's gravitational attraction provides the required centripetal force for the Moon to orbit the Earth

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Predict Motion Without Centripetal Force
nodes.outcome: Predict the straight-line tangential path an orbiting body would take if the centripetal gravitational force ceased to act

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: State Universal Law of Gravitation
nodes.outcome: State Newton's Universal Law of Gravitation in words

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Write Gravitational Force Formula
nodes.outcome: Write the mathematical formula F = G * M * m / d^2 and define each variable in it

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: State Value and SI Unit of G
nodes.outcome: State the numerical value (6.673 x 10^-11 N m^2/kg^2) and SI unit of the universal gravitational constant G

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Apply Inverse Square Law
nodes.outcome: Calculate the factor by which gravitational force changes when the distance between two masses is doubled or halved

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Apply Mass Proportionality to Force
nodes.outcome: Calculate the factor by which gravitational force changes when one or both masses are altered

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate Gravitational Force Between Two Masses
nodes.outcome: Calculate the magnitude of the gravitational force between two specified masses at a given distance using F = G*M*m/d^2

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: List Phenomena Explained by Universal Law
nodes.outcome: List the four key natural phenomena explained by the Universal Law of Gravitation (binding to Earth, planetary orbits, lunar orbit, ocean tides)

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Mechanism of Ocean Tides
nodes.outcome: Explain how the differential gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun on Earth's oceans causes high and low tides

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Retention of Earth's Atmosphere
nodes.outcome: Explain that Earth's gravitational pull prevents atmospheric gas molecules from escaping into space

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Free Fall
nodes.outcome: Define free fall as the motion of an object falling toward Earth under the influence of gravitational force alone

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Acceleration Due to Gravity
nodes.outcome: Define acceleration due to gravity (g) as the uniform acceleration experienced by a freely falling body near Earth's surface

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: State SI Unit of g
nodes.outcome: State the SI unit of acceleration due to gravity (g) as m/s^2

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Distinguish Between g and G
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between the universal gravitational constant (G) and acceleration due to gravity (g) in terms of constancy, units, and nature

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: State Mass Independence of Free Fall
nodes.outcome: Explain that all freely falling bodies experience the same acceleration regardless of their masses when air resistance is absent

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Derive Formula for g on Earth Surface
nodes.outcome: Derive the relation g = G * M / R^2 from Newton's Second Law and the Universal Law of Gravitation

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate Numerical Value of g on Earth
nodes.outcome: Calculate the numerical value of g (~9.8 m/s^2) on Earth's surface by substituting G, mass of Earth, and radius of Earth

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Variation of g with Earth's Shape
nodes.outcome: Explain why the value of g is greater at the poles than at the equator based on Earth's flattened spherical shape and equatorial radius

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Variation of g with Altitude
nodes.outcome: Explain why the value of g decreases as altitude above Earth's surface increases using the inverse-square relation

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Write Kinematic Equations for Vertical Motion
nodes.outcome: Write the three equations of motion for vertical free fall by replacing acceleration 'a' with 'g' and distance 's' with height 'h'

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Apply Sign Conventions for Free Fall
nodes.outcome: Assign correct signs to initial velocity, displacement, and acceleration (+g downward, -g upward) in vertical motion problems

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate Maximum Height Reached
nodes.outcome: Calculate the maximum height reached by an object thrown vertically upward given its initial launch velocity

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate Time of Ascent and Descent
nodes.outcome: Calculate the time taken by a vertically projected object to reach maximum height and the total time of flight

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate Impact Velocity of Dropped Object
nodes.outcome: Calculate the final velocity and time taken for an object dropped from a specified height upon hitting the ground

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Mass as Measure of Inertia
nodes.outcome: Define mass as the quantity of matter in a body and a measure of its inertia

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: State Constancy of Mass
nodes.outcome: State that mass of an object remains constant everywhere in the universe and never changes with location

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify SI Unit and Tool for Mass
nodes.outcome: State the SI unit of mass (kg) and identify a pan balance (beam balance) as the instrument used to measure it

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Weight as Gravitational Force
nodes.outcome: Define weight as the force with which an object is attracted toward the center of the Earth (or celestial body)

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: State Formula and SI Unit of Weight
nodes.outcome: Write the formula W = m * g and state that the SI unit of weight is the Newton (N)

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify Vector Nature of Weight
nodes.outcome: Explain that weight is a vector quantity having magnitude and a direction directed vertically downwards toward the center of the Earth

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Describe Measurement of Weight
nodes.outcome: Describe how a spring balance measures weight by measuring the gravitational pull on an object

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Variation of Weight with Location
nodes.outcome: Explain why the weight of an object changes from place to place (e.g., equator to pole, Earth to Moon) while its mass remains constant

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Compare Mass and Weight
nodes.outcome: Distinguish between mass and weight across definition, SI unit, scalar/vector nature, variability, and measuring instrument

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Derive Moon-to-Earth Weight Ratio
nodes.outcome: Derive the ratio showing that the weight of an object on the Moon is approximately 1/6th of its weight on Earth using the Universal Gravitation formula

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate Weight of Object on Moon
nodes.outcome: Calculate the weight and mass of an object on the Moon given its mass or weight on Earth

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Thrust
nodes.outcome: Define thrust as the total perpendicular force exerted on a surface, with SI unit Newton (N)

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Pressure and State Formula
nodes.outcome: Define pressure as thrust per unit area (Pressure = Thrust / Area)

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Pascal as SI Unit of Pressure
nodes.outcome: State the SI unit of pressure as N/m^2 (Pascal, Pa) and define 1 Pascal

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Relate Pressure Inversely to Contact Area
nodes.outcome: Explain how pressure varies inversely with contact area for a constant thrust force

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Wide Straps on School Bags
nodes.outcome: Explain why school bags are provided with wide straps to reduce pressure on shoulders using the pressure-area relationship

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Sharp Edge Cutting and Sharp Pins
nodes.outcome: Explain why sharp knives cut more effectively and pointed nails penetrate surfaces more easily than blunt ones

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Broad Feet of Camels
nodes.outcome: Explain why camels can walk easily in sand due to broad feet exerting smaller pressure

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate Pressure Exerted by a Block
nodes.outcome: Calculate the pressure exerted on a surface by a rectangular block resting on different faces given dimensions and mass

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: State Pressure Exertion in Fluids
nodes.outcome: State that fluids (liquids and gases) exert pressure in all directions on any object immersed and on container walls

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Pressure Variation with Fluid Depth
nodes.outcome: Explain why fluid pressure increases with depth beneath the surface of the liquid

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Buoyancy and Upthrust
nodes.outcome: Define buoyant force (upthrust) as the upward force exerted by a fluid on an object immersed in it

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Apparent Loss of Weight in Liquids
nodes.outcome: Explain why objects feel lighter when immersed in water due to the upward buoyant force opposing gravity

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify Factors Affecting Buoyant Force
nodes.outcome: Identify that the magnitude of buoyant force depends on the volume of the submerged object and the density of the fluid

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Compare Downward Weight and Buoyant Force
nodes.outcome: Predict whether an immersed object moves upward or downward by comparing gravitational force (weight) and buoyant force

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: State Floating and Sinking Density Rule
nodes.outcome: State the rule that an object floats if its density is less than fluid density and sinks if its density is greater than fluid density

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Floating of Cork and Sinking of Nail
nodes.outcome: Explain why an iron nail sinks in water while a cork floats by comparing their densities with the density of water

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Predict Floating/Sinking from Given Density
nodes.outcome: Predict whether a given material will float or sink in a specified liquid given numerical density values of both

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: State Archimedes' Principle
nodes.outcome: State Archimedes' Principle: an object immersed fully or partially in a fluid experiences an upward force equal to the weight of fluid displaced

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate Buoyant Force Using Displaced Fluid
nodes.outcome: Calculate buoyant force from the mass or volume of fluid displaced by a submerged body

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Floating of Heavy Iron Ships
nodes.outcome: Explain using Archimedes' principle why a huge iron ship floats on ocean water while a tiny iron nail sinks

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: List Applications of Archimedes' Principle
nodes.outcome: List engineering and scientific applications of Archimedes' Principle including lactometers, hydrometers, ships, and submarines

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Working of Lactometer and Hydrometer
nodes.outcome: Explain how lactometers test milk purity and hydrometers determine liquid density based on Archimedes' principle

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Relative Density
nodes.outcome: Define relative density as the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of water at 4 degrees C

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Dimensionless Nature of Relative Density
nodes.outcome: Explain why relative density is a pure dimensionless number without any physical units

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate Relative Density from Substance Density
nodes.outcome: Calculate relative density of a substance given its density (or mass and volume) and density of water (10^3 kg/m^3)

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate Substance Density from Relative Density
nodes.outcome: Calculate absolute density of a substance in SI and CGS units from its given relative density value (e.g., silver RD = 10.8)

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Force Intuitively
nodes.outcome: Define force intuitively as a push or a pull acting upon an object.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: List Observable Effects of Force
nodes.outcome: List the observable effects of applying a force on an object, including changing its speed, direction of motion, or shape.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Identify Force as a Vector Quantity
nodes.outcome: Identify that force is a vector quantity possessing both magnitude and direction.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Balanced Forces
nodes.outcome: Define balanced forces as equal and opposite forces acting simultaneously on an object such that their resultant net force is zero.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Relate Balanced Forces to Zero Acceleration
nodes.outcome: Explain why balanced forces do not produce any change in the state of rest or uniform motion of an object.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Deformation by Balanced Forces
nodes.outcome: Explain how balanced forces can change the shape or size of an object even when its state of motion does not change.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Unbalanced Forces
nodes.outcome: Define unbalanced forces as forces acting on an object whose resultant net force is non-zero.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Calculate Net Force in One Dimension
nodes.outcome: Calculate the net resultant force acting on an object subjected to multiple collinear forces.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Classify Balanced and Unbalanced Scenarios
nodes.outcome: Classify everyday physical scenarios (like a tug-of-war or pushing a heavy box) into balanced or unbalanced force systems.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Link Unbalanced Forces to Acceleration
nodes.outcome: Explain why an unbalanced external force is necessary to accelerate an object or change its direction of motion.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Frictional Opposing Force
nodes.outcome: Explain how the force of friction between surfaces opposes motion and prevents a box from sliding until the applied force exceeds friction.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Describe Galileo's Single Incline Observation
nodes.outcome: Describe Galileo's observation of a marble rolling down an inclined plane gaining speed and rolling up losing speed.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Describe Galileo's Double Incline Experiment
nodes.outcome: Describe Galileo's thought experiment showing that a marble released on a double inclined plane seeks to reach the same original height.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Deduce Galileo's Law of Motion on Horizontal Surface
nodes.outcome: Deduce Galileo's conclusion that an object on a frictionless horizontal plane would continue to move with constant velocity forever without any net force.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: State Newton's First Law of Motion
nodes.outcome: State Newton's First Law of Motion verbatim or in equivalent precise standard language.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Distinguish the Two Parts of the First Law
nodes.outcome: Identify the two separate conditions in Newton's First Law: an object at rest remaining at rest, and an object in uniform motion continuing along a straight line.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Define Inertia
nodes.outcome: Define inertia as the natural tendency of an object to resist a change in its state of rest or of uniform motion.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Classify the Three Types of Inertia
nodes.outcome: Classify inertia into inertia of rest, inertia of motion, and inertia of direction.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Everyday Inertia of Rest Phenomena
nodes.outcome: Explain why passengers fall backward when a bus starts suddenly using the concept of inertia of rest.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Coin and Playing Card Experiment
nodes.outcome: Explain why a coin drops vertically into a tumbler when the card beneath it is flicked sharply.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Carrom Stack Behavior
nodes.outcome: Explain why striking the bottom coin of a carrom stack allows the remaining pile to remain intact and fall vertically.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Carpet Beating via Inertia
nodes.outcome: Explain why beating a hanging carpet with a stick dislodges dust particles.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Everyday Inertia of Motion Phenomena
nodes.outcome: Explain why passengers lurch forward when a moving bus brakes abruptly using inertia of motion.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Safety Function of Seatbelts
nodes.outcome: Explain how safety belts protect vehicle passengers during collision or sudden braking based on inertia of motion.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Athlete Run-Up Before Long Jump
nodes.outcome: Explain why a long jumper runs a certain distance before taking off in terms of inertia of motion.

nodes.subject: Science
nodes.title: Explain Everyday Inertia of Direction Phenomena
